body.text: 26 U.S.C. § 174 governs the federal income tax treatment of research and experimental (R&E) expenditures for U.S. taxpayers. The TCJA required amortizing domestic costs over five years and foreign costs over 15 years starting in 2022; the 2025 OBBBA added Section 174A, restoring immediate domestic expensing after 2024, while foreign research remains subject to mandatory 15-year amortization.
Executive Overview of the Section 174 Statutory Regime

Title 26 U.S. Code Section 174 governs the federal income tax treatment of Research and Experimental (R&E) expenditures, establishing the statutory framework that determines whether corporate innovation costs are recovered immediately or capitalized and amortized over multi-year recovery periods. Under the capitalization framework enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97) and taking effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, taxpayers were stripped of the long-standing option to immediately deduct qualifying research costs as ordinary business expenses. Instead, the amended statute mandated that all Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures be charged to a capital account and amortized ratably over a five-year (60-month) period for domestic research activities, or a fifteen-year (180-month) period for foreign research activities, beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which those expenditures are paid or incurred.

The transition from immediate expensing to mandatory capitalization fundamentally altered the financial mechanics of corporate research across the United States, converting a structural innovation incentive into a broad federal revenue-raising mechanism. Beyond accelerating cash tax liabilities, the Section 174 capitalization regime generated cascading compliance complexities across the broader tax code: it reshaped the calculation and coordination of the Section 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities, complicated financial statement tax provision reporting and Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) valuation under Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 740, and created severe multi-state compliance friction where state taxing authorities—most notably the California Franchise Tax Board (FTB)—explicitly decoupled from federal law. Subsequent federal legislation, specifically the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21, signed into law on July 4, 2025), further bifurcated the regime by enacting Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174A to restore immediate domestic R&E expensing for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while leaving the 15-year mandatory amortization period intact under Section 174 for foreign research expenditures.
Statutory Evolution of Section 174 Across Three Eras
The 1954 Statutory Safe Harbor (1954–2021)

Prior to the enactment of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, the federal tax code lacked a dedicated statutory provision governing research and development expenditures. In the absence of explicit statutory authority, federal courts consistently ruled that product research and development costs were capital in nature because they were incurred to create assets yielding long-term economic value. Under that pre-1954 judicial doctrine, corporate taxpayers were required to capitalize research outlays and hold them in suspense accounts until the underlying project either definitively failed—permitting the taxpayer to claim an abandonment loss under IRC Section 165—or succeeded, resulting in a capital asset amortizable over its determinable useful life. As documented in the 1954 House legislative report, where research projects were not abandoned and where a definite useful life could not be determined, taxpayers had no statutory means of amortizing or recovering their research expenditures.

Congress enacted IRC Section 174 in 1954 specifically to eliminate this pervasive friction and accounting confusion between the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and corporate taxpayers, and to subsidize the technical risk inherent in industrial innovation to stimulate economic growth, technological advancement, and American competitiveness. From 1954 through taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022, Section 174 operated as a flexible statutory safe harbor offering taxpayers two primary recovery pathways. Under pre-TCJA Section 174(a), taxpayers could elect to immediately deduct R&E expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year as ordinary and necessary business expenses akin to IRC Section 162. Alternatively, under pre-TCJA Section 174(b), taxpayers could elect to treat R&E expenditures as deferred expenses chargeable to a capital account (resulting in a basis adjustment under IRC Section 1016) and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months, or elect under IRC Section 59(e) to deduct R&E expenditures ratably over a 10-year period. In addition, software development costs enjoyed a protective administrative safe harbor under Revenue Procedure 2000-50 prior to 2022, which permitted immediate expensing without strict adherence to the Section 174 technological uncertainty tests. For nearly seven decades, this immediate expensing architecture allowed capital-intensive manufacturers and pre-revenue startups to optimize cash flows by offsetting taxable income directly with current developmental costs.
The TCJA Mandatory Capitalization Era (2022–2024)

When Congress enacted the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Pub. L. 115-97) in 2017, it sought to broaden the federal tax base and offset the significant revenue losses associated with lowering the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21%. To achieve this budgetary offset, Congress amended IRC Section 174 on a delayed effective date, making mandatory capitalization applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021.

The TCJA amendments fundamentally rewrote the statutory mechanics of Section 174 by stripping taxpayers of the option to immediately expense R&E expenditures and reclassifying qualifying outlays as Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures chargeable to a capital account. Under amended Section 174(a)(2)(B), all domestic SRE expenditures were required to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a five-year (60-month) period, beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenses were paid or incurred. Simultaneously, Congress introduced a severe geographic penalty by subjecting expenditures attributable to foreign research activities (research conducted outside the United States) to a 15-year (180-month) amortization period. This three-fold increase in recovery length established a protectionist tax policy designed to penalize the offshoring of intellectual property development and incentivize the repatriation of high-value research roles to the United States. Furthermore, the TCJA added Section 174(c)(3), establishing a statutory mandate that all software development costs be automatically treated as SRE expenditures, thereby eliminating the Rev. Proc. 2000-50 safe harbor and sweeping standard technology sector development outlays into the capitalization requirement regardless of whether the software was intended for internal use or commercial sale.

Because the statutory midpoint convention limits first-year cost recovery to six months of amortization in a standard twelve-month taxable year, a five-year (60-month) domestic amortization schedule stretches across six taxable years, yielding a 10% (6/60) deduction in Year 1, 20% (12/60) annually in Years 2 through 5, and the final 10% (6/60) in Year 6. Similarly, the 15-year (180-month) foreign amortization period stretches across sixteen taxable years, permitting only a 3.33% (1/30) deduction in Year 1, 6.67% (1/15) annually in Years 2 through 15, and the final 3.33% (1/30) in Year 16.
The 2025 OBBBA Restoration and Section 174A (2025 Onward)

The working-capital strain and cash flow disruption caused by the TCJA capitalization mandate between 2022 and 2024 led to sustained lobbying from the technology, pharmaceutical, and manufacturing sectors, culminating in the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21) on July 4, 2025. Section 70302 of the OBBBA partially restored the original intent of the 1954 legislation by enacting a new provision, IRC Section 174A, applicable to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, which permits the immediate expensing of domestic R&E expenditures under Section 174A(a), explicitly including domestic software development costs under Section 174A(d)(3). In addition to immediate expensing under Section 174A(a), industry tax analyses from Grant Thornton and RSM note that taxpayers may alternatively elect under Section 174A(c) (by the return due date, including extensions) to capitalize domestic R&E expenditures and amortize them ratably over not less than 60 months, or elect annually under conforming amendments to IRC Section 59(e) to amortize domestic R&E expenditures ratably over 10 years (which can also align regular tax treatment with the 10-year Alternative Minimum Tax amortization requirement applicable to individuals and pass-through owners, or increase adjusted taxable income for the IRC Section 163(j) business interest limitation).

However, the 2025 OBBBA retained the TCJA's mandatory 15-year (180-month) capitalization and amortization requirement for foreign research expenditures under narrowed Section 174, cementing a permanently bifurcated tax policy that pairs a domestic innovation incentive with a severe penalty on foreign research outsourcing. Under the OBBBA, the transition back to immediate deductibility under Section 174A is treated as a taxpayer-initiated change in method of accounting made with the Treasury Secretary's consent and applied on a cut-off basis, with no IRC Section 481(a) adjustment for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

To address the stranded capital assets accumulated during the 2022–2024 TCJA window, the OBBBA and IRS procedural guidance (including Revenue Procedure 2025-23, Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32) established three primary recovery pathways alongside modified IRC Section 481(a) transition mechanics:

items: Continued Five-Year Amortization (Default Rule): Taxpayers that choose not to make transition elections continue to amortize their 2022–2024 capitalized domestic SRE expenditures over the remainder of their original five-year (60-month) recovery schedules.

Forward Catch-Up Acceleration (1-Year or 2-Year Election): Any taxpayer may elect to deduct the remaining unamortized balance of domestic R&E expenditures capitalized between 2022 and 2024 either in full in the 2025 taxable year, or ratably over a two-year period across the 2025 and 2026 taxable years.

Small Business Retroactive Election (2022–2024 Amended Returns): Qualifying small business taxpayers meeting the IRC Section 448(c) gross receipts test (defined as having average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less over the prior three taxable years measured from the 2025 tax year, after thresholds of $29 million for 2023 and $30 million for 2024, and excluding tax shelters allocating 35% or more of losses to limited partners or limited entrepreneurs) were permitted to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 by amending their 2022, 2023, and 2024 returns. Under Revenue Procedure 2025-28, this retroactive election was required to be filed by the earlier of July 6, 2026, or the expiration of the IRC Section 6511 claim for credit or refund statute of limitations (such as April 15, 2026, for a 2022 return filed April 15, 2023). Furthermore, under Revenue Procedure 2026-32 (released September 4, 2026), taxpayers that did not properly comply with TCJA Section 174 capitalization in prior years can correct their accounting methods while transitioning to Section 174A through modified IRC Section 481(a) adjustments coordinated with their unamortized basis recovery election.

body.text: Defining Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) Expenditures
Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2 Parameters and the Uncertainty Test

The reclassification of research costs into the Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) category demanded a rigorous reevaluation of corporate cost accounting, capturing a comprehensive spectrum of both direct and indirect costs associated with the innovation lifecycle. The foundational legal definition of qualifying expenditures resides in Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1), which defines R&E expenditures as costs incurred in connection with a taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense".

Under the regulatory text, expenditures satisfy this threshold if they are incurred for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty is legally defined as existing whenever the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability, the optimal method, or the appropriate design for developing or improving the product. Crucially, the ultimate success, failure, commercial viability, sale, or internal use of the product is entirely irrelevant to its eligibility under Section 174, because the statute is structured to address the attempt to resolve technological uncertainty rather than the successful achievement of a commercial solution.

Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2 defines a "product" in expansive terms to encompass any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property, regardless of whether the property is used internally by the taxpayer or held for sale, lease, or license to third parties. Within this framework, a "pilot model" is specifically defined as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty during development. Furthermore, Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(5) establishes the vital "shrink-back" rule, which dictates that if an overarching product does not satisfy the uncertainty test as a whole, the taxpayer must systematically evaluate the expenditures at the component or subcomponent level. The presence of technological uncertainty regarding a specific subcomponent does not automatically qualify the entire overarching system, compelling taxpayers to maintain meticulous cost segregation between experimental subcomponents and routine commercial assemblies.
Explicit Cost Inclusions and Exclusions under IRS Notice 2023-63

Under IRS Notice 2023-63 (published in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2023-39), which serves as the primary executive branch explanatory memorandum for the TCJA-era Section 174 rules, SRE expenditures are defined broadly to capture all direct and indirect costs incident to SRE activities. Specifically, Notice 2023-63 sweeps in comprehensive labor costs (including basic compensation, stock-based compensation, overtime pay, vacation pay, holiday pay, sick leave, payroll taxes, pension costs, and employee benefits for full-time, part-time, and contract employees who perform, supervise, or directly support SRE activities, while explicitly excluding severance compensation), tangible materials and supplies consumed in experimental activities or pilot models, cost recovery allowances (depreciation, amortization, and depletion on testing equipment, servers, and laboratory facilities used in SRE performance), allocable operations and facility overhead (rent, utilities, insurance, property taxes, repairs and maintenance, and security costs allocated via a reasonable cause-and-effect relationship), and travel and patent procurement costs (including attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application).

Conversely, Treasury Regulations and IRS Notice 2023-63 explicitly exclude specific operational and corporate expenses from Section 174 treatment, requiring them to be accounted for under standard IRC Section 162 operating expense rules or other applicable capitalization statutes. General and administrative (G&A) service department costs that only indirectly support research—such as human resources personnel recruiting scientists or accounting departments processing R&D payroll—are excluded from the SRE cost pool. Additionally, interest on debt financing utilized to fund SRE activities, website hosting costs, routine quality control testing, efficiency surveys, management studies, consumer market surveys, and advertising or promotional expenditures do not qualify as SRE expenditures. Land and depreciable or depletable property acquisition costs also remain outside direct Section 174 and Section 174A deduction treatment, except to the extent of annual depreciation or depletion allowances on property used in research.

body.text: The Software Development Mandate (Section 174(c)(3))

One of the most disruptive elements of the TCJA amendments was the absolute inclusion of software development costs within IRC Section 174(c)(3) (and subsequently carried forward for domestic software development under IRC Section 174A(d)(3) by the 2025 OBBBA). Notice 2023-63 provides a comprehensive functional definition of software development activities, stipulating that the planning, designing, building of models, writing of source code, conversion of source code to machine-readable code, and testing of software must all be capitalized as SRE expenditures. Furthermore, work performed on "upgrades and enhancements" that result in additional functionality or materially increase the speed or efficiency of existing software is treated as a capitalizable SRE activity.

To prevent routine Information Technology (IT) operations from being swept into mandatory capitalization, the IRS established explicit boundaries excluding standard operational technology costs. Under Notice 2023-63, activities excluded from Section 174(c)(3) software capitalization encompass the selection and purchase of existing off-the-shelf software, basic installation, configuration (defined strictly as manipulating pre-coded parameters), employee training, data conversion, website hosting, and routine maintenance or debugging that corrects coding errors but does not give rise to new upgrades or enhancements.
Administrative Mechanics Under IRS Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12
Cost Allocation Methodologies and Midpoint Conventions

On September 8, 2023, the Department of the Treasury and the IRS released an advance version of Notice 2023-63 (published in IRB 2023-39), and subsequently modified it on December 22, 2023, via IRS Notice 2024-12, establishing the executive branch interim guidance on the application of the mandatory capitalization and amortization rules prior to the issuance of final regulations. Because modern corporate operations deeply intertwine research and development with general manufacturing and administration, Notice 2023-63 requires taxpayers to allocate overhead and indirect costs to SRE activities using a rigorous methodology that establishes a direct "cause-and-effect relationship" or another reasonable relationship that logically connects the costs incurred to the benefits provided by the SRE activities. While taxpayers are permitted to utilize different allocation methods for different categories of costs—for instance, utilizing labor hours to allocate personnel overhead while using relative square footage to allocate facility rent and building depreciation—the chosen methodology must be applied consistently across the enterprise for that specific cost type.

To operationalize the statutory requirement that amortization begins at the "midpoint" of the taxable year, Section 3 of Notice 2023-63 establishes strict mechanical rules. For a standard 12-month taxable year, the midpoint is unequivocally defined as the first day of the seventh month. The Notice strictly prohibits the acceleration of amortization due to the occurrence of short taxable years, mandating that the 60-month domestic or 180-month foreign recovery periods remain absolute. For taxpayers experiencing a short taxable year, the midpoint month is determined mathematically; if the short taxable year contains an even number of months, the midpoint month is calculated by dividing the number of months by two and adding one:
Consequently, for a 6-month short taxable year running from January through June, the midpoint is the first day of the fourth month ((6 / 2) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4th month, or April 1).
Contract Research: Assessing Financial Risk and Rights to Exploit

Historically, Section 174 lacked explicit statutory rules governing research performed under contract, creating substantial ambiguity for taxpayers offshoring development to foreign subsidiaries or engaging third-party engineering and testing firms. Section 6 of Notice 2023-63, as modified by Notice 2024-12, resolves this ambiguity by establishing a rigorous two-pronged test applied to the "research provider" (the entity performing the research work on behalf of a principal).

Under this two-pronged framework, a research provider must capitalize its incurred fulfillment costs under Section 174 if it satisfies either the financial risk condition or the rights to exploit condition. Under the first prong (Financial Risk), capitalization is triggered if the research provider contractually bears the risk of financial loss should the research fail to produce the desired product, a structure that typically manifests in fixed-price contracts where payment is entirely contingent upon the successful delivery of a functional prototype or software module. Under the second prong (Rights to Exploit), capitalization is triggered if the research provider retains the legal right to use the resulting SRE product in its own trade or business, or to independently exploit the product through sale, lease, or license to third parties. Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12 clarify that "excluded SRE product rights"—which are rights separately bargained for the limited purpose of performing the contracted research for the principal—do not trigger capitalization for the provider.

If the research provider bears no financial risk (for example, operating under a standard time-and-materials contract) and retains no independent rights to exploit the resulting intellectual property, its fulfillment costs are treated as ordinary IRC Section 162 business expenses. Conversely, the "research recipient" (the principal funding the research and retaining the intellectual property) must capitalize the payments made to the provider as its own SRE expenditures under Section 174 (or deduct them under Section 174A if the research is conducted domestically in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024).
Interplay with Long-Term Contracts (Section 460) and Cost Sharing (Section 482)

Notice 2023-63 also addresses the disruptive interplay between Section 174 capitalization and the Percentage of Completion Method (PCM) governing long-term contracts under IRC Section 460. Previously, the immediate expensing of R&E costs could heavily weight the numerator of the PCM calculation, artificially accelerating revenue recognition for defense contractors and heavy manufacturers. Notice 2023-63 provides critical administrative relief by clarifying that taxpayers are only required to include the allowable current-year amortization of SRE expenditures in the numerator of the PCM calculation rather than the entire gross amount of SRE costs incurred, thereby smoothing revenue recognition over the lifecycle of the long-term contract.

With respect to multinational intellectual property structures, Notice 2023-63 addresses Cost Sharing Arrangements (CSAs) under IRC Section 482. The Notice proposes that Cost Sharing Transaction (CST) payments made between controlled participants be treated as a direct reduction of the recipient's Section 174 SRE expenditures chargeable to its capital account, ensuring parity in the capitalization burden proportional to the reasonably anticipated benefits derived from the developed intangibles.
The "Dry Hole" Rule: Section 174(d) Dispositions and Abandonments

Historically, the federal tax code provided a financial safety valve for the inherent risk of unsuccessful innovation: if a research project failed (colloquially termed a "dry hole") or the resulting prototype was abandoned, a taxpayer could claim an immediate abandonment loss under IRC Section 165 to recover the unamortized basis of the investment.

The TCJA eliminated this safety valve entirely through the enactment of IRC Section 174(d), which Section 7 of Notice 2023-63 rigorously enforces: if property with respect to which SRE expenditures were paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the amortization period, no immediate deduction is permitted on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment. Instead, the taxpayer must continue to amortize the SRE expenditures ratably over the remainder of the original 5-year (60-month) or 15-year (180-month) recovery period.

This statutory mandate establishes a fundamental legal separation between the physical or intangible SRE property (such as a physical prototype or software module) and the tax attribute (the SRE expenditure amortization base). For example, a corporation may invest heavily in a software module during Year 1, determine that the code is commercially unviable, and completely abandon the project. Despite the asset ceasing to exist, the corporation must continue amortizing its capitalized development costs on its federal tax returns over the remainder of the 60-month recovery schedule (which, under the midpoint convention where Year 1 and Year 6 each recover 6 months or 10% of the outlay, spans across six taxable years—such as 2024 through 2029—unless accelerated in 2025–2026 under the OBBBA transition elections). This generation of a long-term Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) disconnected from physical reality requires rigorous ASC 740 tax provision analysis, as financial statement auditors must evaluate whether a valuation allowance is required against the DTA based on future cash flow projections and the likelihood of realizing the tax benefit. Furthermore, under the 2025 OBBBA amendments to Section 174(d), for foreign research property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, no deduction or reduction to the amount realized is allowed on account of that disposition, and the 15-year amortization schedule must continue uninterrupted.
Procedural Guidance and Accounting Method Changes

To facilitate the massive transition from immediate expensing to mandatory capitalization, the IRS issued a cascade of Revenue Procedures governing automatic changes in methods of accounting under IRC Section 446. The IRS initially issued Revenue Procedure 2023-8 (subsequently superseded by Revenue Procedure 2023-11 on December 29, 2022, and later modified by Revenue Procedure 2024-9 and Revenue Procedure 2025-8, also cited as Rev. Proc. 2025-08), establishing the administrative procedures for taxpayers to obtain automatic consent to change their accounting methods to comply with TCJA-amended Section 174.

Crucially, the TCJA mandated that this initial accounting method change be applied on a cut-off basis rather than through a traditional IRC Section 481(a) cumulative catch-up adjustment. Under the cut-off rule, mandatory capitalization applied exclusively to SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and no retroactive adjustment or restatement of prior-year R&E deductions was permitted or required.

As interim substantive guidance evolved through the issuance of Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12 (which clarified short taxable year ambiguities and refined contract research definitions), the IRS correspondingly expanded procedural flexibility. Revenue Procedure 2025-8 modified Section 7 of Revenue Procedure 2023-11 to permit taxpayers to file successive automatic accounting method changes for taxable years starting in 2022 through 2024. This administrative flexibility allowed corporations to continuously restate and refine their capitalized SRE cost pools in response to evolving IRS Notices without bearing the administrative burden of filing complex non-automatic Form 3115 requests. Following the enactment of the 2025 OBBBA, the IRS issued Revenue Procedure 2025-23, Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32 (employing Designated Change Numbers 265 for TCJA Section 174 changes, 273 for Section 174A domestic changes and transition methods, and 274 for foreign research expenditures), whereby transitioning back to immediate domestic deductibility under IRC Section 174A is executed as a taxpayer-initiated change in accounting method applied on a cut-off basis for newly incurred post-2024 domestic costs, while unamortized capital balances accumulated between 2022 and 2024 and prior method corrections are recovered through acceleration elections and modified Section 481(a) adjustments.
Interplay Between Section 174 and the Section 41 R&D Tax Credit
Structural Comparison: Section 174 SREs vs. Section 41 QREs

While IRC Section 174 (and IRC Section 174A for post-2024 domestic research) governs the deduction and capitalization of research expenditures, IRC Section 41 governs the tax credit available for increasing research activities. The statutory provisions are inextricably linked and must be analyzed synchronously because the foundational requirement under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) for any expense to qualify for the Section 41 R&D credit is that it must first be an expenditure eligible for treatment as a research expenditure under Section 174—or, following the OBBBA conforming amendments to Section 41(d) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, eligible to be treated as a domestic R&E expenditure under Section 174A (commonly termed the "Section 174 / Section 174A test").

However, the pools of qualifying costs are far from identical; Section 41 operates as a much narrower statutory filter. Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under Section 41 represent a tightly restricted subset of the broader Section 174 SRE / Section 174A R&E pool. While Section 174 SREs capture gross compensation, employee fringe benefits, pension costs, stock-based compensation, and payroll taxes, Section 41 domestic employee compensation is restricted strictly to Form W-2, Box 1 wages. Foreign research expenditures must be capitalized and amortized over 15 years under Section 174, yet are excluded entirely from the Section 41 credit calculation. Similarly, 100% of qualifying U.S.-based contract research is capitalized under Section 174 (or deducted under Section 174A) where risk or rights apply, whereas Section 41 statutorily limits eligible contract research to 65% of the actual expense (with enhanced statutory rates in certain state regimes, such as Texas's higher education contract research rate). While laboratory supplies and qualifying development cloud computing costs are eligible under both statutes, capital depreciation allowances, patent attorneys' fees, and allocated facility overhead (rent, utilities, and insurance) must be capitalized under Section 174 under Notice 2023-63 but are completely excluded from the Section 41 credit base. Finally, funded R&D where the researcher retains neither financial risk nor exploitation rights is capitalized by the funding recipient under Section 174, while remaining excluded from the researcher's credit base under the IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion.

body.text: The "Substantially All" Rule and the Process of Experimentation

To transition an expenditure from a Section 174 SRE (or Section 174A domestic R&E) into a Section 41 QRE, the underlying research must satisfy a rigorous four-part statutory test under IRC Section 41(d): in addition to meeting the Section 174 / Section 174A test (requiring technical uncertainty under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1)), the activity must be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature (relying on principles of the physical sciences, biological sciences, computer science, or engineering under Section 41(d)(1)(B)), must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (improving functionality, performance, reliability, or quality rather than style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors), and must undergo a genuine "process of experimentation" under Section 41(d)(1)(C).

IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) mandates that "substantially all"—defined statutorily and regulatorily as at least 80%—of the research activities measured on a business component basis must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. A valid process of experimentation requires a systematic scientific methodology that identifies a technological uncertainty, formulates hypotheses, designs an experiment (through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial-and-error), conducts the test, and evaluates the resulting data. If 80% or more of the activities on a business component satisfy the process of experimentation test, then the remaining 20% of the activities (even if they involve routine supporting tasks such as basic styling or documentation) may also qualify as QREs, provided they satisfy the baseline Section 174 requirements.
Coordination and the Section 280C(c) Election

Taxpayers claiming the Section 41 R&D credit must also navigate statutory anti-double-dipping rules under IRC Section 280C(c). Historically—and once again under the OBBBA's conforming amendment to Section 280C(c) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024—a taxpayer is required to reduce its domestic Section 174 / Section 174A deduction or capitalized expenditure base by the dollar amount of the Section 41 research credit claimed. Under mandatory capitalization, reducing the Section 174 or Section 174A amortization base creates intricate downstream tracking burdens because the taxpayer must bifurcate its capital accounts.

Alternatively, taxpayers may make an irrevocable annual election under IRC Section 280C(c) on a timely filed original tax return (or on an amended 2022–2024 return for eligible small businesses retroactively applying Section 174A under the OBBBA transition rules) to claim a reduced research credit, which reduces the credit by the 21% maximum corporate tax rate. Opting for the reduced credit allows the corporate taxpayer to maintain its full, gross Section 174 or Section 174A deduction and amortization base intact, substantially simplifying deferred tax asset accounting under ASC 740. However, with the introduction of the redesigned IRS Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024, with updated Instructions Rev. December 2025) and its new Section G (Business Component Information), the IRS has substantially increased the compliance documentation burden, requiring granular business-component-level reporting and detailed breakdowns demonstrating how claimed QREs map directly to capitalized SREs or Section 174A deductions, demanding complete synchronicity between a taxpayer's R&D credit study and its Section 174 / Section 174A capitalization model.
State-Level Conformity Frameworks and Decoupling Mechanics
The California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) Decoupling Strategy

As federal research tax law underwent structural shifts under the TCJA and the 2025 OBBBA, individual state jurisdictions exercised their sovereign authority to either conform to the updated Internal Revenue Code or decouple from it based on their statutory conformity dates. The State of California, administered by the Franchise Tax Board (FTB), stands as the most prominent nonconformity jurisdiction in the United States.

California operates under a "fixed date" statutory conformity framework. For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2015—and continuing through the 2023, 2024, and 2025 California filing instructions—California law generally conforms to the Internal Revenue Code as it existed on January 1, 2015. Consequently, California explicitly ignores the TCJA's Section 174 capitalization mandate: for California state income and franchise tax purposes, both domestic and foreign R&E expenditures remain fully deductible as current operating expenses in the taxable year they are paid or incurred. Furthermore, the FTB has clarified that California does not conform to the TCJA terminology of "Specified Research or Experimental Expenditures," nor does it conform to the 2025 OBBBA's Section 174A amendments. Under the California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC), taxpayers continue to operate under the historical, pre-TCJA version of Section 174. While this deliberate decoupling preserves a substantial state-level cash tax advantage for R&D-intensive enterprises operating in California, it forces corporate tax departments to maintain deeply bifurcated accounting systems: one set of capitalization and amortization schedules for federal purposes, and a parallel set of immediate expensing schedules for state purposes.
FTB Form Adjustments and Entity-Level Impacts

To reconcile this statutory divergence, taxpayers must manually adjust their California state tax returns each year to account for the federal-to-state variance. Across California Form 100 (California Corporation Franchise or Income Tax Return), Form 100S (California S Corporation Franchise or Income Tax Return), Form 565 (Partnership Return of Income), and Form 568 (Limited Liability Company Return of Income), taxpayers must identify the federal Section 174 amortization deduction taken on the federal return, add that amortized amount back to their state income calculation, and subsequently deduct the full, gross amount of R&E expenditures incurred during the taxable year to arrive at California net income.

For estates and trusts filing California Form 541 (California Fiduciary Income Tax Return), specialized rules govern the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) on Schedule P (541) (Alternative Minimum Tax and Credit Limitations – Fiduciaries). While pre-TCJA IRC Section 174(a) allows a fiduciary to claim a full immediate deduction in the taxable year paid or incurred for California regular tax purposes, those R&E expenditures must be amortized over a 10-year period for California AMT purposes (unless the estate or trust makes an optional write-off election under IRC Section 59(e) in the year of the expenditure, which applies the 10-year write-off period for regular tax and eliminates the AMT adjustment on Schedule P (541)). Consequently, absent an IRC Section 59(e) election, the fiduciary must compute the California AMT adjustment by subtracting the 10-year AMT amortization from the regular tax immediate deduction and reporting the difference on Schedule P (541).

Furthermore, for pass-through entities (PTEs) electing to pay the California PTE Elective Tax (utilized to bypass the federal state and local tax deduction cap and reported on Forms FTB 3893, FTB 3804, and FTB 3804-CR, Pass-Through Entity Elective Tax Credit), the calculation of Qualified Net Income (QNI) relies strictly on the California definition of net income. Because immediate R&E expensing under California law substantially reduces the entity's QNI baseline relative to federal income, it directly reduces the 9.3% PTE elective tax liability and the corresponding 9.3% tax credit passed through to the partners, members, or shareholders.

body.text: State R&D Credit Distinctions and Texas Comptroller Interpretations

California's nonconformity extends beyond deduction mechanics into the computation of its state-level Research and Development Tax Credit. Although the California R&TC heavily references federal IRC Section 41, it applies a distinct, geographically bounded definition of "gross receipts" when calculating the base amount of the state credit. For California purposes, gross receipts include only sales of real, tangible, or intangible property held for sale to customers in the ordinary course of business that are delivered or shipped to a purchaser located within California, while explicitly excluding service-related receipts, rents, or interest. This substantially lower gross receipts denominator can yield a significantly larger California R&D tax credit for technology and software companies that incur heavy R&D payroll in California but generate primarily service or Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) revenue from out-of-state customers. Other states, such as Connecticut, utilize entirely different statutory thresholds, whereas New York and Pennsylvania maintain their own distinct structural interactions with Section 174 that require localized analysis.

State executive branch interpretations in Texas have similarly clarified the boundary between Section 174 and state R&D credits. In Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts administrative memorandum 202503003M (STAR Accession No. 202503003M, issued March 24, 2025), taxpayers under audit or refund verification argued that because the acquisition expenses of certain prototypes or tangible assets could be deducted under IRC Section 174, those outlays should automatically qualify as non-depreciable "supplies" under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C) for purposes of the Texas Franchise Tax R&D credit under Texas Tax Code Section 171.651. The Texas Comptroller explicitly rejected this argument, ruling (with citations to TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278, and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-084) that qualification as an IRC Section 174 expenditure under Section 41(d)(1)(A) is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for an expense to constitute a Qualified Research Expense (QRE). If tangible property is depreciable in the taxpayer's hands under IRC Section 167, it remains statutorily excluded from the definition of supplies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C), regardless of its eligibility under Section 174.
Judicial Interpretation and Landmark Case Law

Federal appellate courts and the U.S. Tax Court have established the controlling judicial guardrails governing what constitutes a valid Section 174 expenditure, how depreciable property exclusions operate in the context of commercial prototypes and tooling, and what level of documentation is required to substantiate technical uncertainty and a process of experimentation.
TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner (133 T.C. 278)

In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), the U.S. Tax Court evaluated the intersection of IRC Section 174 (R&E expenditures), IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C) (supply QREs), and IRC Section 167 (depreciation). The taxpayer, an injection-molded automotive parts manufacturer, hired third-party toolmakers to construct production molds based on the taxpayer's internal engineering designs, bearing the economic risk that the molds would fail to meet customer specifications. The IRS challenged the inclusion of these mold costs, contending that because physical molds are durable tangible assets, they constituted "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under Section 174(c) and Section 41(b)(2)(C), which barred them from treatment as R&E expenditures and rendered them ineligible as QRE supplies under Section 41.

The Tax Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer, establishing the precedent that the statutory phrase "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" takes its meaning from IRC Section 167 and must be interpreted contextually to mean property that is depreciable in the hands of the specific taxpayer claiming the expense. Because TG Missouri ultimately sold the molds to its automotive customers—with legal title passing upon completion and customer acceptance—the molds were classified as inventory or cost of goods sold rather than depreciable capital assets in TG Missouri's hands. Consequently, the expenditures were not barred by Section 174(c) or Section 41(b)(2)(C) and were validly claimed as research supply expenses, severely limiting the IRS's ability to categorically exclude third-party production prototypes and tooling from Section 174 treatment.
Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287)

While TG Missouri protected prototype and tooling outlays, the Seventh Circuit's 2023 decision affirming the Tax Court in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), issued a stringent warning regarding contemporaneous documentation and the rigid application of the IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) "process of experimentation" test. In that case, a shipbuilding enterprise claimed substantial R&D credits for the development of a novel "first-in-class" vessel and a dry dock, which the IRS disallowed in full on the ground that the taxpayer failed the 80% "substantially all" process of experimentation requirement.

The Seventh Circuit held that although direct support and supervision labor can legally be included in the numerator of the 80% test (provided the supervisors are actually overseeing specific elements of an experimental process), the taxpayer failed structurally by refusing to apply the regulatory "shrink-back" rule. Instead of isolating the specific subcomponents of the vessel that contained genuine technological uncertainty during the design spiral, the taxpayer attempted to claim the entire physical vessel as a single, monolithic business component pilot model. Because the taxpayer lacked granular, contemporaneous time-tracking data tying employee hours directly to the experimental iterations of specific subcomponents, it could not prove that 80% of the activities associated with the entire vessel were experimental. By explicitly rejecting "shortcut estimates" and broad departmental allocations, Little Sandy Coal established that qualification under Section 174 is merely the starting line and that taxpayers must modularize their documentation down to the subcomponent level to survive judicial scrutiny.
Fairchild Industries v. United States (71 F.3d 868) and Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113)

In the realm of contract research, Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1996), remains the controlling appellate ruling on the "funded research" exclusion under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H), which directly informs the financial risk and exploitation rights parameters of Section 174. The Federal Circuit held that research is not considered "funded"—and therefore remains eligible for the research credit and treatment as the researcher's Section 174 expenditure—if payment to the researcher is contingent on the ultimate technical success of the research. This holding established the legal standard now codified in Section 6 of IRS Notice 2023-63, mandating that financial risk must be contractually borne by the entity claiming the primary research tax attribute.

Subsequent 2024 judicial decisions—including the Eighth Circuit's ruling in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (2024) denying credits to a structural engineering firm under the funded research exclusion, and the U.S. Tax Court's ruling in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (decided December 23, 2024)—continue to reinforce strict compliance boundaries for engineering design contracts. In Phoenix Design Group, the Tax Court evaluated three sampled projects (a military psychiatric unit, a hospital, and a university engineering and science building) designed by a mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering firm. The Tax Court denied the claimed research credits and sustained accuracy-related penalties, holding that to satisfy the Section 174 test, a taxpayer must prove both that objectively available information did not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the product, and that the taxpayer engaged in investigative activities to discover information eliminating that uncertainty. Performing standard engineering calculations on available data (such as sizing ductwork from airflow data) or complying with building codes does not constitute an investigative activity under Section 174 or a process of experimentation under Section 41(d), nor can a failed system-level claim shrink back merely to a design phase or specific employees' activities. Together with Fairchild and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Phoenix Design Group underscores that taxpayers face severe disallowance and penalty exposure when their commercial contracts shift financial risk and IP rights away from the claiming entity or when they lack documentary evidence of a systematic evaluation of technical alternatives.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: Federal Amortization vs. California Expensing

During the 2024 taxable year, hypothetical taxpayer TechNova Inc. generates $50,000,000 in gross profit prior to accounting for research and development costs and incurs $10,000,000 in domestic software development costs. These software development outlays qualify in full as Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures under federal IRC Section 174(c)(3) and as deductible R&E expenditures under California's pre-2015 IRC conformity rules.

Under the federal TCJA capitalization mandate, TechNova Inc. is legally prohibited from deducting the $10,000,000 software outlay as a current operating expense. Instead, it must charge the $10,000,000 to a capital account and amortize it ratably over 5 years (60 months). Applying the mandatory midpoint convention established under Section 174(a)(2)(B) and Section 3 of IRS Notice 2023-63, TechNova Inc. is permitted to amortize only 10% of the expenditure (representing 6 months out of the 60-month recovery period) in Year 1:

Conversely, for California franchise and income tax purposes, the California FTB does not conform to the TCJA capitalization mandate and permits TechNova Inc. to immediately expense the entire $10,000,000 software development outlay in Year 1. Reconciling from federal taxable income on California Form 100, TechNova Inc. adds back the $1,000,000 federal amortization deduction (+$1,000,000) and deducts the full $10,000,000 current-year R&E expenditure (−$10,000,000), resulting in a net California schedule adjustment of −$9,000,000 and a Year 1 California taxable income of $40,000,000:

Year 1 California Taxable Income: $50,000,000 (Gross Profit) − $10,000,000 (CA R&E Deduction) = $40,000,000

body.text: In this single taxable year, the legislative divergence between federal and California law causes TechNova Inc. to report a federal taxable income ($49,000,000) that is $9,000,000 higher than its California taxable income ($40,000,000)—and in enterprises with narrower pre-R&E operating margins, federal taxable income can easily exceed double the state taxable income. This requires TechNova Inc.'s corporate tax department to track a $9,000,000 Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) base for federal ASC 740 financial reporting purposes while managing the cash flow consequences of substantially higher federal tax liabilities. Furthermore, should TechNova Inc. abandon this software project in 2025 (and not elect OBBBA catch-up acceleration), federal rules under IRC Section 174(d) dictate that the remaining $9,000,000 unamortized basis cannot be written off as an abandonment loss; instead, the $9,000,000 must continue to be amortized ratably on federal returns through 2029 even though the underlying software code no longer exists.
Multidisciplinary Substantiation and Technical Compliance Architecture

Traditional accounting firms frequently approach R&D studies purely as a financial accounting and payroll categorization exercise, relying on high-level departmental cost allocations that fail the strict judicial substantiation standards established by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner and the U.S. Tax Court in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner.

In contrast, deploying specialists who hold advanced degrees in software engineering, physical sciences, and manufacturing enables direct technical communication with a taxpayer's engineering staff in their native discipline. This technical capability is essential to isolate component-level technological uncertainties under the Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(5) shrink-back rule and to delineate routine post-deployment maintenance or debugging from qualifying Section 174 and Section 174A software "upgrades and enhancements" as defined by IRS Notice 2023-63. Coupled with proprietary tax technology that tracks unamortized DTA basis under ASC 740, evaluates optimal IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit elections, maps QREs to SREs for Section G of the redesigned Form 6765, and automates federal-to-state reconciliation schedules required by nonconforming jurisdictions such as California, this integrated methodology bridges the gap between raw technological development and audit-defensible tax compliance.
Conclusions

Title 26 U.S. Code Section 174, enacted in 1954 as a straightforward statutory safe harbor to encourage immediate expensing of research outlays, has evolved into a highly complex, multi-layered regulatory and accounting regime. The TCJA's mandate to capitalize and amortize domestic and foreign research beginning in 2022—and the subsequent partial reversal introduced by the 2025 OBBBA via Section 174A—have permanently altered corporate financial planning, forcing enterprises to strictly segregate SRE expenditures from ordinary operating expenses. IRS Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12 reinforce this regime through strict midpoint conventions, two-pronged contract research risk and rights assessments, and the continued amortization of abandoned properties under Section 174(d), while judicial decisions such as Little Sandy Coal, TG Missouri, Fairchild Industries, and Phoenix Design Group demand granular documentation at the subcomponent level. Compounding this federal complexity is widespread state nonconformity, exemplified by California's preservation of pre-2015 immediate expensing rules and Texas's strict exclusion of depreciable assets from supply QREs under Memorandum 202503003M, which provide distinct state tax outcomes at the cost of maintaining parallel multi-year accounting systems. Realizing the full financial benefit of corporate innovation requires treating the Section 41 R&D tax credit, Section 174 and Section 174A cost recovery, and state tax conformity not as isolated calculations, but as a unified corporate tax engineering strategy.
